That was originally forced -- continuo had no shipped hook -- and it is now KEPT deliberately: this PR ships src/fencing/hook.mjs, but a renderer case needs only "the context names a script file that exists", and reaching for the shipped hook here would couple the case to the hook's own file layout while making the space-bearing path impossible. entries.target_id: test/fencing/renderer.test.ts::renders > the default hook launcher resolves on this platform
entries.reason: Was not-ported in the PR that translated this file, on the premise that continuo had no shipped hook script to resolve. THIS PR SHIPS src/fencing/hook.mjs, so the premise is gone and the case is translated. Three of the source's four assertions carry across unchanged: default_hook_script() -- defaultHookScript() here, pointing at the shipped hook.mjs -- names a file that exists; the launcher resolves on THIS platform (`Path(ctx.python).is_file() or shutil.which(ctx.python)`, both halves); and the render SUCCEEDS rather than refusing hook-unresolvable, which the source calls the actual regression. ADAPTED for the fourth: the source asserts `ctx.python == (sys.executable or "python3")`, the running PYTHON interpreter. continuo's hook is a Node script (D-0204), so FenceContext.python defaults to process.execPath -- a recorded deviation documented at the field itself -- and there is no "python3" fallback because process.execPath is always an absolute path. The assertion is NOT dropped: it is replaced by the one that means the same thing here, `expect(ctx.python).toBe(process.execPath)` -- the default IS the running interpreter. That substitution of a Python-interpreter identity for its Node equivalent is the whole of the adaptation.

intentional_divergences.topic: The renderer decided that a hook command invokes interlock's deny hook by a SUBSTRING test, so a command that merely mentions the hook path -- without executing it -- was admitted. continuo requires the hook to be the program that actually runs.
intentional_divergences.status: intentional divergence; continuo is authoritative (D-0208; D-0022 is superseded by D-0023: interlock is frozen, so an inherited defect is repaired at the first belt that touches it)
intentional_divergences.direction: interlock renders a document continuo refuses
intentional_divergences.reproduction: renderer.py:412 is `if str(ctx.hook_script) in hook["command"]:`. A command such as `/bin/echo <hook_script> --role worker --fence <fence_path>` therefore satisfies every check the renderer makes: `_check_command_resolves` finds `/bin/echo` on PATH and finds the script token on disk, `_check_invocation` finds `--fence` and `--role` carrying the right values, and the matcher is universal. The CLI then runs `echo` and the deny hook never executes, so the render succeeds and the session is unfenced.
intentional_divergences.measurement: Measured against interlock at 65f36c5 rather than reasoned about: driving `render_fence` with exactly that command returns a fence of 17 rules. The same 17-rule render was measured in continuo before this change, and again by reverting the new check to the substring test; after the change both the `/bin/echo` shape and the `true` shape refuse with `hook-absent`. Re-measured when the argv[0] branch was dropped, on the same four shapes: the `/bin/echo` decoy refuses `hook-absent` before and after; the `true` decoy refuses `hook-absent` before and after; the shipped `{python} {hook_script}` shape renders 17 rules before and after; the bare `{hook_script}` shape at argv[0] goes from rendering 17 rules to refusing `hook-absent` at mode 0755 (and from `hook-unresolvable` to `hook-absent, hook-unresolvable` at the shipped mode 0644). All 45 renderer cases were then run under one fixed order seed with every refusal's codes logged: the log differs in exactly one line, the added refusal from the rewritten target-only case, so no ported case changed its refusal codes.
intentional_divergences.detail: continuo now tokenises the command with the CPython `shlex.split` transcription (D-0200) and treats it as invoking the deny hook only if the hook script is argv[1] AND argv[0] is `ctx.python` -- the interpreter the renderer itself recorded, which is what `{python} {hook_script} ...` renders to. That is the ONLY accepted shape. An earlier form of this divergence also accepted the hook script at argv[0] (a directly executable hook); that branch was dropped before the change shipped, because it was open on Windows. The shipped src/fencing/hook.mjs has no shebang and is mode 0644: on POSIX `checkCommandResolves` refuses it `hook-unresolvable` via access(X_OK), but on Windows X_OK is only an existence check, so the render SUCCEEDED there, `cmd` cannot execute a .mjs directly, the deny hook never launched, and the child ran UNFENCED with the spawn recorded as admitted (Windows is a required CI cell, D-0003). The argv[0] shape is one nothing produces -- all four shipped roles render `{python} {hook_script} ...`, and interlock's own hook.py is likewise not executable -- so requiring the recorded interpreter is strictly tighter at no cost, and closes the hole on every platform instead of special-casing one. POSITION ALONE IS NOT SUFFICIENT: `true /path/hook.mjs --fence X --role worker` puts the hook at argv[1] and would satisfy a naive position check, because `true` resolves on PATH exactly as `echo` does; it is the `argv[0] === ctx.python` half that rejects it. The shipped src/fencing/roles.json is unaffected -- all four roles already use the `{python} {hook_script} ...` form and all four still render -- and none of the 40 ported source cases changes its refusal codes (verified by execution, before and after). The divergence is fail-closed and stays traceable here because parity is still judged against interlock. Originally recorded as an inherited limitation, disclosed and not repaired under D-0022, and surfaced by an independent review of this port (Codex); D-0023 superseded that rule when interlock was frozen, and the defect is repaired here because this is the first belt that touches the code.

intentional_divergences.topic: An unparseable hook command refuses with one code in interlock (rule-syntax) and two in continuo (rule-syntax, hook-absent). The second half of D-0208: tokenising the command first means a command that does not tokenise is not counted as invoking the deny hook.
intentional_divergences.status: intentional divergence; continuo is authoritative (D-0208). Fail-closed: continuo refuses strictly more loudly about a document interlock also refuses.
intentional_divergences.direction: both refuse; continuo reports an additional code
intentional_divergences.reproduction: Render the worker role with `hooks.PreToolUse[0].hooks[0].command` set to `{python} {hook_script} --role worker --fence "{fence_path}` -- the shipped command shape with one unbalanced double quote. interlock's `_check_command_resolves` raises rule-syntax on the shlex failure, and because its invocation test is a SUBSTRING match the command still counts as invoking the hook, so hook-absent is never reached. continuo's `commandRunsHook` tokenises with the CPython shlex transcription (D-0200) and returns false on the ShlexError, so `interlockMatchers` stays empty and `hook-absent` -- "no PreToolUse hook invokes Interlock's deny hook" -- is appended after the same rule-syntax.
intentional_divergences.measurement: Measured by execution, with set EQUALITY rather than containment so the extra code is the thing asserted: the target-only case below observes exactly {rule-syntax, hook-absent} against continuo. interlock's single code is read off renderer.py at 65f36c5, where the substring test at line 412 is what keeps hook-absent unreachable on this input.
intentional_divergences.detail: No ported case pinned this on either side before now, which is why it is added: D-0208's prose already mentioned the behaviour, but a divergence that no case measures is a claim, not a fact. intentional_divergences.topic: A rendered `sandbox.filesystem.denyRead` / `denyWrite` entry that is not a string. interlock's renderer emits whatever its repair leaves behind and has no post-condition on it; continuo refuses the fence outright, because CLI 2.1.261 answers such an entry by applying neither `permissions.deny` nor any `PreToolUse` hook for the whole run.
intentional_divergences.status: intentional divergence; continuo is authoritative (D-0093). It belongs here and not in `inherited_limitations` because that list is scoped by docs/test-translation-conventions.md to rough edges the port REPRODUCES rather than fixes, each entry saying what the behaviour is and that it matches the source -- and this behaviour has no source to match: the defect is in the Claude Code CLI, not in interlock, and what continuo adds is a refusal interlock does not make.
intentional_divergences.direction: interlock renders a document continuo refuses
intentional_divergences.reproduction: Outside continuo entirely, against the CLI: a git repository carrying no settings of its own, and `claude -p '<one command>' --settings F --setting-sources '' --model claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 --output-format json`, where F carries one `permissions.deny` rule, one `PreToolUse` Bash hook that writes a witness file BEFORE returning `permissionDecision: deny`, and a `sandbox` block. With `sandbox.filesystem.denyRead: ["/abs/.ssh"]` the hook fires and the command is refused. Re-spell that SAME entry as `[{"path": "~/.ssh"}]` -- or as `[42]`, or move it to `denyWrite` -- and the witness file is never written, so the hook was not invoked and overruled, it was never invoked; the denied command runs. Exit zero, no warning, nothing on stderr. The witness file is the whole observation: its absence is the direct evidence that the pipeline was discarded rather than consulted.
intentional_divergences.measurement: Measured against CLI 2.1.261 (node v22.17.0, Linux/WSL2), not reasoned about: 36 cells. A 24-cell matrix of 8 `sandbox` spellings x 3 commands (`git worktree list`, `ls -la <dir>`, `touch <file>`, each with its matching `Bash(...)` deny rule). The four spellings whose deny entries are all strings -- the key absent, `{enabled:true, filesystem:{denyRead:["/abs/.ssh"]}}`, the same without `enabled`, and the same plus an unknown sibling key -- fire the hook and refuse the command in every cell. The four carrying a non-string entry -- `denyRead:[{"path":"~/.ssh"}]` with and without `enabled`, `denyWrite:[{"path":"~/.ssh"}]`, and `denyRead:[42]` -- fire no hook and run the command in every cell. 8 supplementary cells (`additionalDirectories` as `["<abs>"]`, `[{"path":"<abs>"}]`, `[42]`, `[null]`, x 2 commands) are ALL harmless: the hook fires and the command is refused, so a non-string there voids nothing, and the refusal is scoped away from it deliberately. 4 further cells with matcher `*` and `deny: ["Read(<secret>)", "Edit(<dir>/**)"]` show the void is not Bash-only: under the flat spelling both the `Read` and the `Write` are refused by the hook; under the dict spelling the `Read` SUCCEEDS and returns the file's contents, and the `Write` is refused only by the nobody-to-approve path, not by the rule. The decisive pair was repeated 4x each, 4/4 both ways; the remaining cells were run once. Held constant and therefore unmeasured: one CLI version, one platform, `claude -p` only, one model, and a `--settings` file with `--setting-sources ''` as the only delivery route.
intentional_divergences.detail: ONE mechanism, not two defects: continuo #131 (a denied read-only command runs and the bytes arrive) and #130 (the write refused by the missing-approval path rather than by the rule) are the read and write halves of the same voided pipeline, and docs/operations/lap-1-dogfood.md section 9.5 F-8 recorded them as two. "Read-only commands bypass the fence" was never the variable; an unparseable sandbox deny list is. The repair is a POST-CONDITION, `checkRenderedSandboxDenyStrings(rendered, role)` in src/fencing/renderer.ts, called immediately after `repairSandbox()` and before `settingsPayload()`, refusing `sandbox-entry-not-string` for every offending entry rather than the first. It is a REGRESSION FENCE over D-0082's repair, not a live-hole patch in the renderer: `renderFence` runs `repairSandbox` on every fence it returns, and `parseSandboxEntry` (src/fencing/rules.ts:311-319) and the flattener test the same predicate over the same object graph, so a non-string entry is not reachable from an authored role document today -- and D-0082's own safety rested on a comment saying "unreachable", with nothing enforcing it. A SECOND PRODUCER IS OUT OF SCOPE AND NAMED RATHER THAN LEFT SILENT: src/settings/generator.ts (public API via src/index.ts) writes a child settings file and deliberately passes a non-string deny entry through verbatim in two branches, on the premise -- stated in its own doc comment -- that the launcher surfaces the operator's error and the CLI rejects the whole file. The measurement shows the file is accepted and the fence voided in silence, so that premise does not hold for these two arrays on 2.1.261. It is a live exposure, left for its own issue because repairing it moves parity/settings.settings-generator.ledger.json and because the generator is not a fence. WHY NO EXISTING CASE COULD HAVE CAUGHT THIS CLASS: the breach battery never observes a child -- its evaluator is the fence object's own `decide()` -- so a green battery proves self-consistency inside this process and never CLI enforcement.
intentional_divergences.tracking: suisya-systems/continuo#131, with #130 as the write half of the same cause and F-8 in docs/operations/lap-1-dogfood.md section 9.5. docs/operations/upstream/cli-sandbox-deny-voids-permissions.md is the report, filed upstream as anthropics/claude-code#92365 (https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/92365); #131 stays open until that issue resolves, because this divergence exists only while it does. The generator exposure named in `detail` is the follow-up this entry hands on.

inherited_limitations.topic: The second assertion of test_the_fencing_package_does_not_import_the_discarded_transport_module is nearly vacuous.
inherited_limitations.detail: The source reads `assert "sandbox_by_pattern" not in text or "DISCARDED" in text or '\"\"\"' in text`. The third disjunct is true of any file containing a docstring, which in that package is every file, so the assertion cannot fail on the sandbox_by_pattern axis. The first assertion (about transport.descriptor) is real and does the work. The translation reproduces the disjunction rather than strengthening it, because a port that quietly improves on its source is no longer a parity port and the difference would be invisible to anyone comparing the two suites. A fix belongs upstream, or in a change that moves both sides together. Separately from the inherited vacuity, the TRANSLATED half of this case lost its coverage of src/fencing/hook.mjs when the glob was written as `.ts`-only and the hook shipped as `.mjs`: measured, with `transport.descriptor` appended to hook.mjs a `.ts`-only glob reported this case GREEN. Repaired by globbing `.ts` and `.mjs`. Cross-reference: this is one of three cases in this port where the suite was green while proving nothing; the three are written up together in docs/test-translation-conventions.md, section 10 ("Make it fail on purpose, and confirm it fails for the reason you expect").

inherited_limitations.topic: JavaScript has one number type, so a role document's numeric values can lose both their int/float distinction AND, beyond 2^53, their exact value.
inherited_limitations.status: REPAIRED (continuo D-0095, completing D-0210/D-0211/D-0212/D-0213/D-0214) for every value that reaches a durable artefact or a renderer refusal from a document parsed with `pyJsonLoads`. Two surfaces that parse with `JSON.parse` by design, and two runtime boundaries, are enumerated at the end and are not closed by it.
inherited_limitations.detail: Two distinct losses, both at `JSON.parse`, both inherited from the runtime rather than introduced by the translation. (1) TYPE: Python's json preserves int vs float (`1` and `1.0` parse to different types), so a refusal naming a value's type reads `got int` here where interlock says `got float`. (2) VALUE: an integer beyond `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` is rounded -- `9007199254740993` parses as `9007199254740992` -- and `pyJsonDumps` then emits a number that is neither what was authored nor what Python would print. Because the settings payload is compared byte-for-byte across a restart, a document carrying such a value would render a fence that disagrees with interlock's bytes. No ported case exercises either: the shipped roles.json carries no number in any position that reaches a message or the payload, and the refusal CODE -- which is what the ledger and an operator act on -- is unaffected in every case. Recorded rather than papered over, and raised with the operator: closing (2) means either a lossless number parser or REFUSING an out-of-range number, and refusing is a deliberate divergence from interlock (which accepts it) rather than a bug fix, so it is not a translator's call. Surfaced by an independent review of this port (Codex). Tracked for post-parity repair in suisya-systems/continuo#18, which also carries the upstream decision to take before interlock is archived. REPAIR (D-0095, suisya-systems/continuo#18's last inherited item). The repair ran in two stages and this entry is the record of both. D-0210 through D-0214 closed the SERIALISER half: `pyJsonLoads` rescans the source text and records each number's Python spelling (`int`/`float` by CPython's syntactic rule, plus the literal digits) on its container slot, every container rebuild carries the record across, `pyJsonDumps` re-emits the spelling and `pyTypeNameOf` answers `got float` from the DOCUMENT. That closed loss (1) for a refusal's TYPE and loss (2) for every value that leaves through `json.dumps`. D-0095 closes the three doors that were not `json.dumps`, each of which was still writing JavaScript's answer into an artefact compared BY BYTES. (a) `str()`: `role_kind` and `permission_mode` are read out of the role body and converted with `pyStr`, which fell through to `String` for a number -- so `"role_kind": 1.0` persisted `"1"` against interlock's `"1.0"`, `9007199254740993` persisted the rounded double, and `1e400` persisted `"Infinity"` where Python's `str()` writes `inf`. Both fields are wire fields of the persisted fence (D-0201) and are what `diffFences` compares. (b) The settings payload's `permissionMode`: `settingsPayload` copies the RAW authored value (the source annotates it `str` and never coerces, which this port reproduces), and `permission_mode` is a META key, so `stripMeta` had already removed the slot its spelling hung on. Measured: CPython writes `"permissionMode": 1.0` into `settings.local.json` and this port wrote `1`. The spelling is now carried from the role body to the payload as a value, and only while the value is still the AUTHORED one -- the non-interactive promotion (D-0081) substitutes a string literal, which must not inherit it. (c) `repr()` in a refusal detail: `pyRepr` named the value from the double alone, so `unparseable sandbox entry: 1` stood where interlock writes `1.0` and a `permissions.deny` entry past 2**53 was quoted back as a number the document does not contain. `pyRepr` now takes a spelling, its container arms look each child's up themselves (so every nested case is fixed with no call-site change), and `pyReprOf`/`pyStrOf` are the container-and-key forms beside `pyTypeNameOf`. The four renderer/rules sites that hand a bare document number to a refusal carry the index for them; the sites that iterate a `pyIterate` COPY deliberately do not, because that copy drops the index-keyed record by D-0212's proof, and arming it there would arm the stale-record trap that proof describes. `str()`/`repr()` are a DIFFERENT CPython primitive from `json.dumps` for exactly the non-finite three (`inf`/`nan` against `Infinity`/`NaN`), so the repair is a named transcription (`pyNumberText`) rather than a reuse, and both entry points are pinned against CPython 3.12.3 by the differential vector: `pyjson.number_documents` gains a `texts` row per number carrying `str(x)` and `repr(x)` beside the `types` row it already carried, over the same 37 documents (which already include `1e400` and a 400-digit integer). Control: with the spelling dropped from `pyRepr`'s number arm the vector reports 19 divergences, and the `str` column stays green -- the two entry points fail independently, which is why both are recorded. Pinned end to end by five target-only cases in `test/fencing/spawn-precondition.test.ts`, which patch the numeric literals in as TEXT (the JavaScript literal `1.0` IS `1`, so a body built in code carries no spelling and would pass against the unrepaired renderer), drive `FencedSpawner.spawn`, and assert on the BYTES of the published fence and `settings.local.json`. THE CALL-SITE SWEEP, because the first draft of this repair missed one and an independent review (Codex) found it. Every site in `src/fencing` that turns a value into text was classified, not just the ones the measurement had reached. Carrying now: `role_kind` and `permission_mode` (`pyStrOf` off the role body), the settings payload's `permissionMode`, the `permissions.deny`, `permissions.allow` and `sandbox.filesystem.*` entry refusals and the two hook refusals (by the index of the document's own array), `checkPermissionMode`'s mode and its `sorted(allowed)` list, the `forbidden_allow_regex` entry, the `interlockMatchers` list `checkHooks` BUILDS (a rebuild site, so it carries the record it collects), and the four `state.ts` reads and refusals over a persisted fence. NOT carrying, and why: every other `pyRepr`/`pyStr` call in the subsystem is over a value a guard has already established is a STRING (`rules.ts`'s remaining four, `checkForbiddenAllow`'s two matched-entry messages, `checkInvocation`, `battery.ts` throughout), so no number can reach it. TWO SURFACES ARE DELIBERATELY OUT OF REACH, and they are out of reach at the PARSE, not at the refusal: `src/fencing/readback.ts` and `src/fencing/cli_args_allow.ts` both use `JSON.parse` rather than `pyJsonLoads`, each for a reason its own header states -- the readback parses a CLI's `--debug` stdout, and the cli_args allowlist is a continuo-only document with no interlock counterpart and no key-order or number property to preserve. No spelling is recorded for either, so a number in one of their messages is still JavaScript's rendering. Neither is compared by bytes and neither has an interlock counterpart to diverge from; changing either parse would be a change to those modules' own decisions rather than part of this repair. WHAT REMAINS, stated so the status above stays true: the VALUE of an integer past 2**53 is still the rounded double -- the exact digits are recovered for RE-EMISSION only, so arithmetic on it is arithmetic on the rounded value; and a number at the ROOT of a document has no container slot to hang a spelling on, so an integral float there is classified and re-emitted as an int. Every fencing artefact has an object at its root. Both are the runtime boundary the header of `src/fencing/pyjson.ts` states and the differential corpus pins, not the defect this entry opened on.
